Access




UFCStats (via the Greco1899/scrape_ufc_stats mirror, pinned commit)
Every UFC fight’s round-by-round statistics: strikes by target and position, knockdowns, takedowns, submission attempts, reversals, control time
UFCStats.com blocks automated requests with a bot challenge, so the project uses a public mirror instead of working around it


MMADecisions
Each judge’s round-by-round and total scores; media scorecards
Collected with the site owner’s permission, slowly (1.5–3 s between requests) with an honest user agent, every page cached


BestFightOdds
Historical opening and closing betting lines
robots.txt allows crawling; collected politely and cached



Coverage. 4,109 UFC decisions from 2001 to November 07, 2026. Every one has full round statistics. 3,448 have every judge’s round-by-round scores (sparse before 2011; card totals exist for all). 51,355 media scorecards in all. Closing odds cover 94.7% of decisions since 2007.


Show code
cov |> select(year, `Judge round scores` = round_scores, `At least one media score` = media_any) |>
  pivot_longer(-year) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = name)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#1F4E9E", "#E3A008"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Scorecard coverage is thin before 2011",
       subtitle = "Share of UFC decisions each year with full judge round scores / any media scorecard.",
       x = NULL, y = "Share of decisions", caption = SOURCE_CAPTION) +
  theme_robbery()

title: Methodology
text:
Linking the sources
The sources spell names differently (“Jacaré” vs. “Ronaldo Souza”) and can date events a day apart. Fights are matched on event date (±1 day) and both fighters’ names, using fuzzy name similarity in either order.

4,083 links are high confidence.
26 medium-confidence links (nicknames and aliases) were all checked by hand.
14 MMADecisions decisions don’t link, and all of them were later overturned (mostly to no-contests).
The declared winner agrees between the sources in every linked fight.

Data problems found and fixed along the way:

Point deductions. MMADecisions round scores include deductions (109 deductions in 105 fights). A 10-9 round with a point taken from its winner reads 9-9. Deducted points are added back before modeling, so the outcome is each judge’s own call on the round, and the simulation then subtracts them from every simulated card. Only 25 judge-rounds are genuine 10-10s.
Fighter order. UFCStats lists the winner first for fights before March 2010 and the red corner first afterwards. All core models are corner-symmetric, so this doesn’t affect them; analyses where the corner matters use only fights from March 21, 2010 onward.
A handful of cards whose round count disagrees with UFCStats, or whose rounds don’t sum to the card total, are dropped.

title: Methodology
text:
The round model
Unit: one judge’s score of one round (33,444 judge-rounds, 3,620 fights). Outcome: the fighter that judge gave the round to.
Features: A-minus-B differentials for that round only:

knockdowns;
significant strikes by target (head, body, leg), plus clinch and ground premiums;
non-significant strikes;
significant-strike accuracy;
takedowns landed and failed takedown attempts;
submission attempts and reversals;
control time.

No fight result, method or other-round information is used.
Corner symmetry. Red-corner fighters are usually favourites, so a naive model would learn “red corner wins”. Every training round is mirrored (once from each fighter’s side), and every prediction is symmetrised, so swapping the fighters gives exactly 1 − p.
Models (tidymodels):

logistic regression;
regularised logistic regression (glmnet) with nonlinear terms and interactions;
gradient boosting (xgboost).

All are tuned with grouped cross-validation by fight (no fight is split across folds). They’re tested on a time-based split: train 2006–2019, test 2020–2026.


Show code
plot_model_comparison(mt)









All three models beat the naive “significant-strike leader wins” baseline by a wide margin (test accuracy 82.5%–83.0% vs. 75.2%). They’re close to each other.


Show code
plot_round_calibration(mcal)









The final model is xgboost. It gives up about 1% of log-loss to glmnet but is the best calibrated. Calibration matters most here, because round probabilities are combined across rounds and judges, and close rounds are exactly where disputed decisions come from. The reason the linear models lag is visible in the boosted model’s SHAP values: judges’ reward for a strike lead flattens out once a round is clearly won.


Show code
plot_shap_dependence(sd)










What judges reward
For interpretation we use the logistic model, whose coefficients convert into an exchange rate: how many significant head strikes each edge is worth on a judge’s card.


Show code
plot_what_judges_reward(le)

title: Methodology
section: From rounds to a decision: the simulation
text:
From rounds to a decision: the simulation
Judges watch the same fight, so their round calls are correlated. Each judge’s call is modelled as a shared “what everyone saw” factor plus individual noise. That keeps each judge’s own chance of giving fighter A the round equal to the model’s probability, while letting judges agree more often than independent coin flips would. The correlation is estimated by maximum likelihood from how often the three real judges split.


Show code
plot_judge_split(js, fx("rho"), fx("rho_lo"), fx("rho_hi"))









Judges split on 22.0% of rounds. The correlated model predicts 22.2%; independent judges would split 35.9% of the time.
Then, for every fight:

10-8 rounds come from a separate model (P(10-8 | winner of the round), using knockdowns, strikes, control and submission attempts, plus an era flag), with its own between-judge correlation.
10-10 rounds are rare and come from a small model based on round closeness and era.
Out-of-fold probabilities. For fights whose own scorecards were in the training data, round probabilities come from models that never saw that fight (10-fold, grouped by fight).
10,000 sets of three scorecards are simulated. A fighter wins with at least two cards; anything else is a draw. Point deductions are applied.

This gives P(A wins), P(draw) and P(B wins), and the Robbery Score = 1 − P(declared winner wins).
Two checks back this up. A simpler direct fight-level model agrees closely. And on older fights that only have judges’ card totals (never used in training), the simulation predicts each judge’s card winner about as well as on the rest.

title: Methodology
text:
Limitations

Statistics can’t see everything. Damage, power, a fighter being hurt without a knockdown, octagon control and aggression are invisible to the counts. A high Robbery Score means the stats disagree, not that the judges were wrong.
Early data are thinner. Statistics for older fights were coded from video years later, and judges’ round scores and media cards are sparse before 2011. Older entries carry a limited corroboration flag.
Scorecard availability. The round model is trained on fights with judges’ round scores (mostly 2011 onward) and applied to all fights.
Correlated judges are modelled with a single, league-wide correlation.
Corner order on UFCStats is known only from March 2010, so red-corner analyses start there.
Associations, not causes. Every judge, era and market comparison is observational.

title: The 2017 Judging Criteria
text:
In August 2016 the Association of Boxing Commissions (ABC) approved revised scoring criteria for MMA’s Unified Rules (recorded in the rules as amended on August 3, 2016), effective January 1, 2017. The update put effective striking and grappling (impact, damage) first, with effective aggressiveness and octagon control as tiebreakers, and clarified when a 10-8 round should be given. State commissions adopted the changes on their own schedules, so 2017 is partly a transition year.
Sources: Bloody Elbow (2017), Bloody Elbow (2018), BJPenn.com, Uproxx, ABC MMA Officials Handbook.

title: The 2017 Judging Criteria
section: Did the weights judges give to each stat change?
text:
Did the weights judges give to each stat change?
We fit the round model with every statistic interacted with a post-2017 indicator, with standard errors clustered by fight.


Show code
plot_criteria_weights(cr, labs_map, fx("criteria_wald_p"))









The joint test that nothing changed is rejected (χ² = 36.2 on 13 df, p = 0.00056). The same holds when the 2017 transition year is excluded (p = 0.00059). The shifts point the way the new criteria describe:

A knockdown went from about 9.2 to 14.6 head strikes.
A takedown fell from about 2.7 to 1.9.
Ground strikes picked up a premium over distance strikes.
Control time stayed about the same: 2.7 → 3.2 per minute.

In short, impact counts for more, and a takedown on its own for less.

title: The 2017 Judging Criteria
text:
Did 10-8 rounds become more common?


Show code
plot_ten_eight(te)









The raw 10-8 rate rose from 2.4% before 2017 to 3.8% after. Holding the round’s statistics fixed, the odds of a 10-8 were 2.4× higher after the update (95% CI 1.9–3.1). The year-by-year pattern matters more than the average: 10-8s peaked at 6.0% in 2017, then fell back to 1.5% by 2026.

title: The 2017 Judging Criteria
section: Did robberies become more or less common?
text:
Did robberies become more or less common?


Show code
plot_robbery_by_year(rby)









Comparing 2011–2016 with 2017–2026 (years with good scorecard coverage), the Robbery-tier share went from 6.2% to 5.3% (odds ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.62–1.12). The Questionable-or-worse share’s odds ratio is 1.16 (0.95–1.42). There’s no clear change.






WarningAssociations, not causes



Plenty else changed around 2017: fighter styles (more wrestling-heavy and volume-striking approaches), the mix of commissions and venues (including the UFC Apex era), and the pool of judges. These comparisons show what changed alongside the new criteria, not what the criteria caused.

title: Fight Lookup
text:
Each breakdown shows the round-by-round statistics, how each judge scored each round (official scores, so they include any point deductions), and the model’s probability that the official loser won the round. The model only sees that round’s statistics, and treats both corners identically.
Two groups are featured:
Show code
for (grp in levels(fights$group)) {
  cat("\n\n## ", if (grp == "Top robbery") "Top robberies" else "Widely debated decisions", "\n\n", sep = "")
  for (i in which(fights$group == grp)) {
    x <- fights[i, ]
    cat("\n\n### ", fight_label(x$winner_name, x$loser_name), " (", format(x$date, "%Y"), ")\n\n", sep = "")
    media <- if (coalesce(x$media_scored, 0) > 0)
      sprintf("%d of %d media scorecards had %s winning.", x$media_for_loser, x$media_scored, x$loser_name) else
      "No media scorecards are recorded."
    odds <- if (!is.na(x$mkt_p_winner)) sprintf(" Closing betting line: %s was %s (%s implied).",
                                                x$winner_name, if (x$mkt_p_winner >= 0.5) "the favourite" else "the underdog",
                                                pct(x$mkt_p_winner)) else ""
    cat(sprintf("%s · %s decision · **Robbery Score %.3f** (%s) · P(%s wins) = %s, P(draw) = %s.\n\n",
                x$event, x$decision_type, x$robbery_score, x$tier, x$loser_name, pct(x$p_loser), pct(x$p_draw, 0.1)))
    cat(sprintf("Official cards (winner first): %s. %s%s\n\n", x$cards_winner_first, media, odds))
    cat(x$why, "\n\n")
    print(plot_fight_breakdown(x, filter(rounds, fight_url == x$fight_url), filter(judges, fight_url == x$fight_url)))
    cat("\n\n")
  }
}


Top robberies

Igor Pokrajac def. Fabio Maldonado (2012)
UFC on FUEL TV: Korean Zombie vs Poirier · Unanimous decision · Robbery Score 0.998 (Robbery) · P(Fabio Maldonado wins) = 100%, P(draw) = 0.0%.
Official cards (winner first): Jeff Blatnick 29-28; Eric Colón 29-28; Sal D’Amato 30-27. 4 of 5 media scorecards had Fabio Maldonado winning. Closing betting line: Igor Pokrajac was the underdog (43% implied).
Model favored Maldonado in 3 of 3 rounds; Maldonado out-landed Pokrajac 98-36 in sig. strikes (ahead in 3 of 3); Pokrajac had 1 takedown to 0; Pokrajac had 3:20 more control time.

title: The UFC Robbery Detector
text: Every UFC fight that goes to the judges ends with three scorecards, and sometimes a lot of arguing. This project asks a narrower, answerable question: given everything the statistics recorded in each round, how likely was the declared winner to win? When that probability is very low, the stats and the judges strongly disagree. That’s what we call a robbery.

title: The UFC Robbery Detector
text:
The biggest disagreement on record


Show code
plot_fight_breakdown(t1, filter(rounds, fight_url == t1$fight_url), filter(judges, fight_url == t1$fight_url))









Igor Pokrajac def. Fabio Maldonado (May 2012) has the highest Robbery Score of all 4,049 decisions: 0.998. Model favored Maldonado in 3 of 3 rounds; Maldonado out-landed Pokrajac 98-36 in sig. strikes (ahead in 3 of 3); Pokrajac had 1 takedown to 0; Pokrajac had 3:20 more control time.

title: The UFC Robbery Detector
text:
Headline findings

1 in 18 decisions is a statistical “robbery”. Of 4,049 UFC decisions from 2001 to 2026, 225 (5.6%) have a Robbery Score of at least 0.75. Decisions people still argue about land near the top: 11 of 13 widely debated decisions are in the top 16%. See the leaderboard →


What judges reward: a knockdown is worth about 12 significant head strikes, a minute of control about 3.1, and a takedown about 2.2. A body strike counts 0.75 of a head strike and a leg strike 0.59. Shooting for a takedown and missing costs a fighter (-0.67). See the methodology →


The model agrees with the media almost as often as the judges do. Where most media scorecards agreed, the official result matched them 90% of the time and the stats-only model 88%. The Robbery Score correlates with the share of media scoring the fight for the loser at r = 0.59. See the validation →


Judges lean slightly toward the red corner and the betting favourite. On a round the stats call 50/50, judges give it to the red corner +4.7 percentage points more often than the stats alone predict, and to a −300 betting favourite +6.5 points more often. Individual judges, adjusted for how close their rounds were, agree with the stats at very similar rates. See the judges →


The 2017 judging criteria changed what judges reward, but not how often decisions go “wrong”. A knockdown went from about 9 to 15 head strikes and a takedown from 2.7 to 1.9. 10-8 rounds peaked at 6.0% in 2017 and have since faded. Robbery rates show no clear change. See the 2017 analysis →

title: The UFC Robbery Detector
section: How it works, in one paragraph
text:
How it works, in one paragraph
Round-by-round statistics come from UFCStats, and every judge’s round-by-round scorecard plus media scorecards come from MMADecisions (4,109 decisions, 33,444 judge-round scores, 51,355 media scores). A model learns how judges turn a round’s stats into a 10-9, using only that round’s numbers and treating both corners identically. The model’s round probabilities feed a simulation of 10,000 sets of three correlated judges for every fight, which gives the probability that each fighter wins the decision. Full methodology →

Data frozen at November 07, 2026. Built in R with targets; every number on this site is computed from the data at render time.

title: The Robbery Leaderboard
text: The Robbery Score is 1 − P(declared winner wins | fight stats). A high score means the round-by-round statistics strongly favoured the fighter who lost. It does not mean the judges were wrong: stats can’t see damage, power or octagon control. That’s why every row also shows how the media scored the fight, and why some rows carry a limited corroboration flag (fights before 2008, when stats were coded from video years later, or fights with fewer than 3 media scores).

Model favored Green in 3 of 3 rounds; Green out-landed Klose 92-58 in sig. strikes (ahead in 3 of 3); Green had 2:46 more control time. Media: 11 of 14 scorecards had King Green winning.







TipReading a high score



A high score with strong media support for the loser (for example 80–100% of media scorecards) is the clearest kind of disagreement. A high score with little media support usually means the people watching saw something the counts don’t record: damage, power, or which strikes actually landed clean. Those cases are listed on the Validation page.

title: Judges
text:
ImportantHow to read this page



Everything here measures agreement with a statistical model. The model sees only counted statistics, not damage, power or octagon control. A judge who agrees with it less often may simply be weighing those things more. Nothing on this page says any judge is bad, biased or acting in bad faith.
Every judge-level estimate uses judges with at least 100 scored rounds and shrinkage (mixed models with judge random effects), so small samples don’t produce extreme rankings. Intervals are 95%.

title: Judges
section: Do judges agree with the statistics at different rates?
text:
Do judges agree with the statistics at different rates?
Raw agreement rates mislead, because some judges happen to score more close rounds than others. So agreement is measured on a typical round (the model favours one fighter 75/25), adjusted for how close each judge’s rounds were.


Show code
plot_judge_agreement(ja)









Across 49 judges, adjusted agreement ranges only from 73.6% to 77.0% (league average 74.7%), and only 2 judges have intervals that exclude the average. Once you account for how hard their rounds were, judges agree with the stats at very similar rates.

title: Judges
section: Do some judges weigh grappling more than striking?
text:
Do some judges weigh grappling more than striking?
Each judge gets their own multiplier on the striking and grappling parts of the round model (takedowns, control time, submission attempts, reversals).


Show code
plot_grappling(jt)









10 of 49 judges have intervals that exclude the league average, more than the 2–3 you’d expect by chance. So there’s real, if modest, variation in how much individual judges reward grappling relative to striking.

title: Judges
section: The red corner and the betting favourite
text:
The red corner and the betting favourite
On UFCStats the red-corner fighter (usually the more established fighter, or the champion) is listed first, but only from March 21, 2010. Before that the winner was listed first, so corner analyses use only later fights.


Show code
plot_corner_favourite(fav)










Red corner. Controlling for each round’s statistics and both fighters’ UFC experience and record, judges give a statistically even round to the red corner +4.7 points more often (95% CI 3.6 to 5.8). The lean was larger in 2010–2016 (+6.4) than in 2017–2026 (+3.0).
Betting favourite. Using closing odds, judges give a statistically even round to a −300 favourite +6.5 points more often (95% CI 5.2 to 7.8). Controlling for the line shrinks the red-corner lean from +4.9 to +3.7 points, so part of the “red corner” effect is really a “favourite” effect, but not all of it.
Interpretation. Betting markets price things statistics miss: power, durability and reputation. Part of the favourite lean may be judges seeing the same unmeasured quality the market sees. These are associations, not evidence of intent.
Title fights. There’s no clear extra lean toward the red corner (the champion’s corner) in title fights: +1.2 points (95% CI -2.0 to 4.4).
Late-round recency. Winning the final round, by the stats, doesn’t predict the official result beyond the full simulation (p = 0.18). Under round-by-round 10-point-must scoring there’s little room for recency.

title: Judges
text:
Betting markets and “decision risk”
Do bettors account for fighters who tend to win on the cards more than the stats suggest? For each fighter we computed a card premium before every fight: how much more often, on average, they had won earlier UFC decisions than the stats predicted (shrunk toward zero for fighters with few decisions).

Across all fights with odds, a larger premium predicts doing slightly worse than the closing line (coefficient -0.50, SE 0.26).
The effect is concentrated in fights that end early (-1.05, SE 0.39). It’s close to zero when the fight goes to the judges.
One reading: the market slightly overrates records that include generous decisions. This is one exploratory test, so treat it as suggestive.

  transmute(Tier = tier, Decisions = n, `Official winner was the betting favourite` = winner_was_favourite,

  tab_header(title = "Robberies don't systematically go to the favourite",

text: A score is only useful if it lines up with independent evidence. The main test uses media scorecards: journalists who scored the same fights round by round and published their cards on MMADecisions. The model never sees them.

text:
2. Round-level agreement
Media members publish whole-fight scores rather than round-by-round scores, so round-level agreement can only be measured against the judges.
